title: How Scrum Really Runs, from Story Points to Retros
summary: A field guide to the words on your Scrum board: epics, stories, points, Done, the five events and the charts, plus which team tweaks help and which break it.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Sprint planning, Tuesday. Someone points at a ticket and says "that's a 3." The developer means three days. The PO hears three points, which on this team is about a week. QA assumes it includes testing. Nobody's wrong exactly, they're just playing three different games with the same word, and two weeks later the sprint "slips" without anyone having done anything bad.

Most teams that say they "do Scrum" run their own flavor of it, and that's fine. Agile was always meant to be adapted. What hurts is when the words drift apart. This post is a field guide to the shared vocabulary: what the pieces on the board mean, where each idea actually comes from, how teams usually bend it, and which bends break it without anyone noticing. It's written for everyone on the team, whether you're a BA, PO, PM, developer, QA, designer or on day three.

Agile and Scrum are two different things

Agile is a set of values. The Agile Manifesto puts it in four lines: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, responding to change over following a plan. It also says the things on the right still have value. Scrum is one framework for working that way, with its own accountabilities, events and artifacts. You can be agile without Scrum, and you can run every Scrum meeting on schedule without being agile at all.

Epic, story, task, sub-task: what goes where

Here's a detail that surprises a lot of people: the Scrum Guide never mentions epics, user stories, story points or velocity. It talks about Product Backlog items and leaves the rest to you. Everything below comes from practices teams bolted on over the years, mostly from Extreme Programming and tools like Jira, Azure DevOps and Linear. The names change from tool to tool, but the nesting is the same everywhere:

LevelWhat it isTypical size
Initiative / ThemeA business goal that spans quarters. Optional, and many teams skip it.Months
EpicA feature area too big for one sprint, like "saved carts"Several sprints
User StoryA slice a user would notice, small enough to finish in one sprintA few days at most
TaskA piece of work the team needs to deliver a story, often technicalHours
Sub-taskA smaller cut of a task, when it helps split work between peopleA few hours

Two more types show up on almost every board:

  • Bug: something that doesn't work as intended. Size it and rank it like any other item, so fixing bugs doesn't become invisible work.
  • Spike: a time-boxed investigation for when you don't know enough to estimate the real work yet. Its output is an answer, like "the payment SDK supports refunds, here's how," not shipped code.
One rule keeps the levels honest

A story is a unit of value. A task is a unit of work. If a "story" says "set up the database table" and no user would ever notice it, it's a task wearing a story's clothes. If an "epic" fits into one sprint, it's a story. Keep the levels straight and anyone can read the board without a guide.

User stories: a card, a conversation, a check

The usual template looks like this:

The classic template

As a [type of user], I want [something], so that [a benefit].
"As a returning shopper, I want to save my cart, so that I can finish checkout on my phone later."

The template is the least important part. Ron Jeffries described stories in 2001 as three things: a card, a conversation and a confirmation (Essential XP: Card, Conversation, Confirmation). The card is just a token for planning. The real requirement travels through conversation between the people who want it and the people who build it. The confirmation is the set of acceptance tests that show the story works. If your stories are three-page specs that nobody discusses, you've kept the card and lost the other two.

Bill Wake's INVEST checklist from 2003 is still the handiest test for a story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. The one teams forget is Negotiable. Wake is explicit that a story is not a contract for features; the details get worked out together while you build.

Three related terms get mixed up a lot:

  • Acceptance criteria: the checks for one specific story. "Saved cart survives logout. Prices refresh when the cart is reopened." Often written as Given / When / Then.
  • Definition of Ready: a team agreement about when a story is clear enough to pull into a sprint. Handy, but it's a team habit, not part of the Scrum Guide, and a strict one can turn into a gate that blocks conversation.
  • Definition of Done: the quality bar for everything the team ships. The Scrum Guide calls it "a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product." Coded, reviewed, tested, merged, deployed to staging, docs updated, whatever your team agrees. It's the best defense you have against "it's done, it just needs testing."

Status columns: the board is your real process

The columns on your board describe how work actually moves on your team. A common setup:

StatusMeansWho usually moves it
BacklogCaptured, not planned into a sprint yetPO
To DoPlanned for this sprint, not startedTeam
In ProgressSomeone is working on it right nowAssignee
In ReviewBuilt, waiting for code reviewAssignee, then reviewer
In Testing / QAReviewed, being checked against acceptance criteriaQA
DoneMeets the Definition of DoneQA or PO
Two habits that keep the board honest

Move cards when the work moves. A board that's only accurate at 9:30 every morning is a board nobody trusts by 2 p.m. Then limit work in progress. The Kanban Guide says teams "must explicitly control the number of work items in a workflow from started to finished," and pull new work only when there's room. Five half-done tickets are worth less to a user than two finished ones. Stop starting, start finishing.

Story points: useful, often misused

Story points estimate how big a piece of work is compared with other work: effort, complexity and uncertainty rolled together. The team picks a small, well-understood story as a reference ("this is a 2") and sizes everything else against it, usually on a Fibonacci-like scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

The history explains a lot. Ron Jeffries, who says he may have invented them, describes how his XP team first estimated in "ideal days," then multiplied by a load factor that tended to be about three to get real calendar time. Stakeholders kept getting confused by "days" that weren't days, so the team started calling them points (Story Points Revisited). So points were always a planning tool for deciding how much to pull into an iteration. They were never meant to measure people.

Planning Poker, done properly

Mike Cohn's write-up covers the mechanics. The PO explains one item and the team asks questions. Everyone picks a card privately and reveals at the same time, so nobody anchors on the loudest voice. If the numbers differ, the highest and lowest estimators explain first: the high one often knows about hidden work, the low one may know a shortcut. Then you vote again. Don't average the cards, because that hides the disagreement, and the disagreement is the useful part. One to three rounds is usually enough. If a story keeps landing at 13 or above, split it.

Three ways to break story points

First, converting them to hours ("1 point = 1 day"). Then you've got hours with extra steps. Second, using velocity to compare teams or rank people. Jeffries says plainly that "comparing teams on quality of estimates or velocity is harmful," and once velocity becomes a target, points inflate until the number means nothing. Third, treating the estimate as a promise someone gets blamed for missing. If your team gets nothing out of points, Jeffries' own advice is to stop using them. Plenty of teams just count stories instead.

For a longer look at estimation as a conversation, see Agile Estimating and Planning: Treat Every Estimate as a Conversation.

Estimating time and logging work without the surveillance vibe

Many teams, especially ones billing clients or reporting to finance, track hours alongside points. That can be perfectly healthy. A typical Jira-style setup has three fields:

  • Original estimate: the team's first guess for a task, in hours. Set it once and leave it. Rewriting it later to look accurate wipes out the one thing it could teach you.
  • Time logged: actual time spent, recorded as you go. Reconstructing a week from memory on Friday afternoon produces fiction.
  • Remaining: honest time left. This is what feeds the burndown.

Points for stories, hours for tasks. They answer different questions: "how big is this compared with that?" and "how much is left this week?"

Log time to learn, never to rank

Jeffries calls tracking actuals against estimates "at best wasteful," and he has a point when nobody looks at the numbers. If your team does log time, use it to spot where flow breaks: a story that keeps eating review time, a "small" task that always triples. Logging "8h" on a day that was really three hours of work and five of meetings teaches nobody anything. People only log honestly when it's safe to, and it stops being safe the moment the numbers show up in someone's performance review.

The events, and the one job each one has

Scrum has five events: the Sprint itself, plus four inside it. The Scrum Guide gives each a maximum length for a one-month sprint and says shorter sprints usually need less. Refinement isn't an event at all. The guide calls it "an ongoing activity," which is why it ends up scheduled differently on every team.

EventIts one jobTimebox (one-month sprint)
Sprint PlanningAgree on a Sprint Goal, pick the items that serve it and sketch how to build themUp to 8 hours
Daily ScrumDevelopers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust today's plan15 minutes
Backlog RefinementBreak down, clarify and size upcoming items so planning isn't a guessing gameOngoing, no set timebox
Sprint ReviewShow what got built to stakeholders and decide together what comes nextUp to 4 hours
Sprint RetrospectiveFind ways to improve quality and how the team worksUp to 3 hours
The daily, without the ritual

Older versions of the Scrum Guide suggested three questions: what did I do yesterday, what will I do today, what's blocking me. The 2020 guide dropped them. Its rule is simpler: the Daily Scrum is there "to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal," and developers can use whatever format they like. Many teams walk the board from right to left, starting with the items closest to Done, and talk about the work instead of going person by person. Anything that needs a deep dive gets parked for right after. More on this in The Daily Standup That Changes Decisions.

Two other details from the guide are worth knowing. The Sprint Review "is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation," so if your review is twenty slides and zero questions, the stakeholders are watching a show. And the Sprint Goal is the commitment for the sprint, not the list of tickets. During the sprint, "no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal," but scope "may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned."

Keep the retro, whatever else you cut

The retro is the one event that improves all the others. Teams that skip it to "save time" tend to hit the same problems sprint after sprint, because nobody ever sets aside an hour to fix them. Keep it blameless and end with one or two concrete actions, each with an owner and a date. A long wishlist nobody owns is the same as no retro.

Charts: questions to ask, not grades to hand out

The Scrum Guide mentions burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flow as common ways to forecast progress. It also says plainly that they don't replace empiricism. Read each chart as a prompt for a conversation:

ChartWhat it shows and what to look for
Sprint burndownWork remaining against days left. A flat line means nothing is reaching Done. A cliff on the last day usually means cards weren't moved as the work moved.
BurnupWork completed against total scope. Its superpower is showing scope creep: you can see the top line climb mid-sprint.
VelocityPoints finished per sprint. Fine for rough forecasting and spotting trends inside one team. Comparing teams with it doesn't work.
Cumulative flowHow many items sit in each status over time. A band that keeps getting wider, say "In Review," marks your bottleneck.
Work item ageHow long each started item has been in progress. One of the Kanban Guide's four flow measures, and it catches a stuck ticket days before the burndown does.
Charts measure the system

The moment a chart is used to judge individuals, people start working on the chart: padding estimates, splitting tickets to look busy, holding cards in "In Progress" so nothing looks stuck. Use charts to find where the process hurts, fix that together, and move on.

Who does what: three accountabilities, and where everyone else fits

The 2020 Scrum Guide talks about accountabilities rather than roles, and a Scrum Team is "typically 10 or fewer people."

AccountabilityOwns
Product OwnerThe what and the why: the Product Goal, the order of the backlog, and whether the work adds value. One person, not a committee.
Scrum MasterHow the team works: making Scrum effective, coaching, clearing impediments. They lead by serving the team. They're not its manager.
DevelopersThe how: the Sprint plan, the Increment and holding to the Definition of Done. In Scrum terms, "Developers" means everyone who builds the product, including engineers, QA and designers.

BAs and QA usually sit inside the Developers. A BA works with the PO to sharpen stories and acceptance criteria; QA helps define what quality means and checks it. Project Managers aren't a Scrum accountability, but many companies keep them alongside Scrum to handle budgets, contracts and dependencies outside the team. It works best when they look after the edges and leave day-to-day decisions to the team.

What's fine to change, and what breaks it

No real team runs textbook Scrum, and the guide itself says Scrum is "purposefully incomplete." The skill is telling healthy adaptations apart from the ones that remove the feedback loop.

Healthy adaptationAdaptation that breaks it
Adding columns like In Review and QA to match how work really flowsDropping the retro, so the team stops improving
Mixing in Kanban practices (WIP limits, flow metrics) for interrupt-heavy workTurning the daily into a status report for a manager
Picking a sprint length (one to three weeks is common) that fits your release rhythmUsing velocity or points to rank or compare people
Tracking time when the business genuinely needs itSwapping sprint scope mid-sprint whenever someone shouts
Using whatever tool your team actually likesA PO who's never around to answer questions
Scrum or Kanban?

Scrum works in fixed sprints with a goal for each one, which suits product work that benefits from a planning rhythm. Kanban is continuous flow with explicit WIP limits and no sprints, which suits support, ops and work that arrives unpredictably. Pick based on how work actually reaches your team. There's a full comparison in Kanban or Scrum? Start With How Work Reaches Your Team

Try this sprint

  • At the next planning, ask everyone what "a 3" means on this team. If you get three answers, write one down.
  • Read your Definition of Done out loud. If nobody remembers it, rewrite it in five lines or fewer and pin it to the board.
  • Pick one story and check it against INVEST, especially the N: is there still room to talk about the details?
  • Try walking the board right to left at one daily.
  • End the retro with one action, one owner and one date, then open the next retro by checking it.

You don't need a certificate to work well on a Scrum team. You need the same meaning for the same words, and a clear idea of what each meeting is for. Once that's settled, the process stops getting in the way and you get more time for building good software together, a bit better each sprint.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an epic, a story, a task and a sub-task?
faqs.a: They nest from big to small. An epic is a feature area that takes several sprints. A user story is a slice a user would notice, small enough to finish in one sprint. A task is a piece of work needed to deliver a story, usually sized in hours, and a sub-task splits a task further. A handy rule: a story is a unit of value, a task is a unit of work. None of these terms are in the Scrum Guide itself; they come from XP and from tools like Jira.

faqs.q: What is a story point, and how is it different from hours?
faqs.a: A story point sizes work relative to other work, combining effort, complexity and uncertainty. Ron Jeffries, who may have coined them, says they started as "ideal days" multiplied by a load factor of about three, renamed to points because stakeholders found the fake days confusing. Converting points back into hours or using velocity to compare teams defeats the purpose; Jeffries calls comparing teams on velocity harmful.

faqs.q: How do we estimate and log work without it feeling like surveillance?
faqs.a: Size stories in points together, for example with Planning Poker, and estimate tasks in hours if you need to. Log time as you go and keep the remaining figure honest, since it feeds the burndown. Use the data to find where work gets stuck. Once logged hours show up in performance reviews, people stop logging honestly and the numbers lose their value.

faqs.q: What are the Scrum events and how long should they take?
faqs.a: The 2020 Scrum Guide lists the Sprint plus four events, with maximums for a one-month sprint: Sprint Planning up to 8 hours, Daily Scrum 15 minutes, Sprint Review up to 4 hours, Sprint Retrospective up to 3 hours. Shorter sprints usually need less. Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not an event, so it has no fixed timebox.

faqs.q: How much can we customize Scrum before it stops working?
faqs.a: The Scrum Guide calls Scrum purposefully incomplete, so adapting it is expected. Adding board columns, borrowing Kanban WIP limits, choosing your sprint length and tracking time when the business needs it are all fine. The changes that break it remove feedback: skipping the retro, turning the daily into a status report, ranking people by velocity, changing scope in ways that endanger the Sprint Goal, or having a PO who is never available.
